about: The scripted AI lesson (briefs docs/briefs/2026-11-11-scripted-teaching.md and the go-ahead of 2026-11-12): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. All 7 key points and the end quiz.

keyPoints.heading: Electric current — charge on the move

steps.text: Welcome! Today you will find out what is going on inside the wires when you turn something on. Press the button on a torch and its bulb lights at once. In science, a bulb like this is called a lamp.

Inside the metal wires are tiny particles that carry electric charge, which is what flows through the wires. When the torch is on, these particles drift round the wires together. You cannot see the charge, but you can see what it does: it makes the lamp light.
A torch has a cell inside it, the part that pushes the charge round.
In everyday talk a cell is often called a battery. In science, a battery is two or more cells joined together.
The cell, the wires and the lamp, all joined up, make a circuit.

cv-loop.question: The switch in this circuit is open, so there is a gap in the loop. Does the lamp light?
cv-loop.tryShort: Look at the lamp while the switch is open. Then close the switch.
cv-loop.afterTest: While the switch was open, the lamp stayed off. When you closed it, the lamp lit.

explain.promptShort: In one line: why do you think closing the switch made the lamp light?
points: closing the switch made a complete loop
charge can only move round a complete loop

cv-loop.reveal: No: with a gap in the loop, the lamp does not light.

steps.text: The circuit below has a switch, a part that can open a gap in the loop of wire. Predict first: answer the question in the box. Then try the switch to test your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
A complete loop, out of the cell, through the lamp and back to the cell, is called a closed circuit.

steps.question: In a torch, the wire to the lamp comes loose at one end. What happens to the movement of charge?

options.text: It stops everywhere in the loop
It stops only near the loose end
It keeps going, but more slowly

steps.right: Yes. A gap anywhere breaks the loop, and the charge stops moving everywhere at once, not just near the gap.

wrong.M4: Not quite: it stops everywhere in the loop. A gap anywhere breaks the whole loop, so the charge stops moving all the way round, not just next to the gap.
wrong.other: Not quite: it stops everywhere in the loop. With a gap there is no complete loop, so the charge cannot move round at all.

idk.hint: Think about the switch in the circuit above: when it left a gap in the loop, what happened to the movement of charge round the loop?

ask.question: With a gap in the loop, can the movement of charge carry on all the way round the loop?

wrong.other: Not quite.

steps.answerWhy: The movement of charge stops everywhere in the loop. A loose wire leaves a gap, so there is no complete loop and the charge cannot move round at all.

steps.text: A flow of charge is called an electric current. The size of a current is how much charge passes a point in the wire each second.

steps.question: In one second, 2 units of charge pass a point in wire A, and 5 units pass a point in wire B. Which wire has the bigger current?
steps.right: Yes. More charge passes each second in wire B, so wire B has the bigger current.

wrong.other: Not quite: wire B. Current is how much charge passes each second, and 5 units a second is more than 2.

idk.hint: Current is about how much charge passes each second. Look at the two wires again: in which one does more charge pass each second?

steps.answerWhy: Wire B has the bigger current. Current is how much charge passes a point each second: 5 units a second in wire B is more than 2 in wire A.

steps.text: Charge is counted in a unit called the coulomb, written C.
Current is measured in a unit called the ampere, written A, or amp for short. One ampere means one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.

steps.question: A wire carries 3 coulombs of charge past a point every second. What is the current, in amperes?
steps.right: Yes: 3 A. One coulomb each second is one ampere, so 3 coulombs each second is 3 amperes.

wrong.upside-down: Not quite: it's 3 A. It looks as if you divided 1 by 3. One coulomb each second is one ampere, so 3 coulombs each second is 3 amperes.
wrong.other: Not quite: it's 3 A. One coulomb each second is one ampere, so 3 coulombs each second is 3 amperes.

idk.hint: Here, 3 coulombs pass each second. How many amperes is that?

steps.answerWhy: The current is 3 A. One coulomb each second is one ampere, so 3 coulombs each second is 3 amperes.

steps.text: Current is measured with an ammeter, a meter that shows the current in amperes.
An ammeter is joined into the loop itself, so the charge moves through it.

cv-same-current.question: The circuit has two ammeters in the same loop, one on each side of the lamp. How do their readings compare?

options.text: One reads less, because the lamp uses some current up
options.short: One reads less, as the lamp uses some up

options.text: The one nearer the cell reads more
options.short: The one nearer the cell reads more

cv-same-current.tryShort: Read both ammeters. Then open the switch and read them again.
cv-same-current.afterTest: With the switch closed, both ammeters showed the same reading. With it open, both showed 0 A.

explain.promptShort: In one line: why do you think both ammeters read the same?
points: charge is not used up in the lamp
the same current goes all the way round

steps.text: Predict first: answer the question in the box below. Then a circuit opens so you can check your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
In a single loop, a circuit with only one path round, the current is the same at every point, because charge is not used up on the way round.
The total amount of charge that passes a point is called the charge flow. Its symbol is Q, and it is measured in coulombs. It depends on two things: the current, and how long the current lasts.

The equation for charge flow is Q = I t: charge flow = current × time. Q is the charge flow in coulombs (C), I is the current in amperes (A) and t is the time in seconds (s). Writing I t means I multiplied by t.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see how it is done, one step at a time.

steps.prompt: In one line, in your own words: what is an electric current?
points: a flow of charge
how much charge passes a point each second
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: a current is a flow of charge, and its size is how much charge passes a point each second.

steps.question: A torch is switched on. Where in its single loop is the current biggest?

options.text: It is the same everywhere in the loop

steps.right: Yes. In a single loop the current is the same at every point: no part of the loop has more.

wrong.M4: Not quite: it is the same everywhere. Being nearer the cell makes no difference in a single loop.
wrong.M2: Not quite: it is the same everywhere. The lamp does not use current up, so there is no more before it than after it.
wrong.other: Not quite: it is the same everywhere in a single loop.

idk.hint: Think back to the two ammeters in the loop. Where in the loop is the current biggest?

ask.question: Did the two ammeters, on each side of the lamp, show the same reading?

wrong.other: Not quite.

steps.answerWhy: The current is the same everywhere in the loop. Charge is not used up on the way round, so no point has more current than another.

keyPoints.heading: Potential difference and resistance — push and opposition

steps.text: Next: what decides how big a current is. Connect a lamp to one cell and it glows dimly. The brighter a lamp glows, the bigger the current through it.

cv-add-cell.tryShort: Tap Add a cell and watch the ammeter and the lamp.
cv-add-cell.afterTest: With two cells, the ammeter reading went up and the lamp got brighter.

explain.promptShort: In one line: why do you think a second cell changed the current?
points: two cells push the charge harder
a harder push drives a bigger current

cv-add-cell.reveal: The ammeter reading rises and the lamp gets brighter.

options.text: The ammeter reading rises and the lamp gets brighter
options.short: The reading rises and the lamp gets brighter

options.text: The lamp gets brighter but the ammeter stays the same
options.short: The lamp gets brighter; the reading stays the same

options.text: Only the current next to the new cell goes up
options.short: Only the current near the new cell goes up

steps.text: Predict first: answer the question in the box below. Then add a cell to test your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
Any part of a circuit, such as a lamp, is called a component.

The push that drives charge through a component, from one end of it to the other, is called the potential difference across it. Two cells give a bigger potential difference than one, and a bigger push drives a bigger current.
Potential difference is measured in a unit called the volt, written V. Cells joined one after the other add their potential differences together.

steps.question: A single torch cell has 1.5 V across it. What potential difference do two of these cells give, in volts?
steps.right: Yes: 3 V. Two cells give twice the push of one.

wrong.M5: Not quite: 3 V. Two cells give a bigger potential difference than one: 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3 V.
wrong.other: Not quite: 3 V. Two cells give twice the push of one: 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3 V.

idk.hint: Each cell gives 1.5 V of push. What do two lots of 1.5 V add up to?

steps.answerWhy: Two cells give 3 V: 1.5 V + 1.5 V.

steps.text: A voltmeter is the meter that measures potential difference. A voltmeter is joined across a component, with one of its wires at each end of the component, not into the loop.
Try it: in the circuit below, a voltmeter is joined across the lamp, with one wire at each end of it. Add a cell and watch the voltmeter. Tap Next when you are done.
Another name for potential difference is voltage.

steps.question: You want to find out how hard the charge is being pushed through a lamp. Which meter do you use?

options.text: Either: they measure the same thing

steps.right: Yes. How hard the charge is pushed is the potential difference, and that is what a voltmeter measures.

wrong.M8: Not quite: a voltmeter. The push is the potential difference, which a voltmeter measures. An ammeter measures something different: the current, how much charge passes each second.
wrong.other: Not quite: a voltmeter. The push is the potential difference, which a voltmeter measures.

idk.hint: How hard the charge is pushed is the potential difference. Which meter do you use to measure that push?

steps.answerWhy: A voltmeter. How hard the charge is pushed is the potential difference, and a voltmeter measures potential difference.

steps.text: Next, a new component: a resistor, a small part that charge has to pass through, which changes how much current flows.

cv-resistor.tryShort: Put the resistor into the loop and watch the ammeter and the lamp.
cv-resistor.afterTest: With the resistor in, the ammeter reading went down and the lamp got dimmer.

explain.promptShort: In one line: why do you think the lamp got dimmer?
points: the resistor let less current through
less current makes the lamp dimmer

cv-resistor.reveal: The current goes down and the lamp gets dimmer.

steps.text: Predict first: answer the question in the box below. Then put the resistor into the loop to test your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
A resistor limits the current: it makes it harder for charge to get through. How hard a component makes it for charge to get through is called its resistance.
Resistance is measured in a unit called the ohm, written Ω.
The picture below puts it all together: a loop with a resistor in it, an ammeter in the loop, and a voltmeter joined across the lamp.

steps.question: Components X and Y each have 6 V across them. X has a bigger resistance than Y. Which one has the bigger current?

options.text: Both the same, as they have the same potential difference

steps.right: Yes: Y. For the same potential difference, the bigger the resistance, the smaller the current.

wrong.other: Not quite: Y. Resistance makes it harder for charge to get through, so for the same push, the bigger resistance gets the smaller current.
wrong.same: Not quite: Y. The same potential difference does not mean the same current: the bigger resistance gets the smaller current.

idk.hint: The bigger current goes through the component that lets charge through more easily. Which one has the bigger current?

ask.question: Which one lets charge through more easily: X, with the bigger resistance, or Y?

wrong.other: Not quite.

steps.answerWhy: Y has the bigger current. For the same potential difference, the bigger the resistance, the smaller the current, so Y, with the smaller resistance, has the bigger current.

steps.text: The current depends on two things: a bigger potential difference gives a bigger current, and a bigger resistance gives a smaller current.

Potential difference, current and resistance are linked by one equation: V = I R, potential difference = current × resistance. V is the potential difference in volts (V), I is the current in amperes (A) and R is the resistance in ohms (Ω). In the equation, the letter V means the potential difference, not the unit.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see how it is done, one step at a time.

steps.question: A lamp has a potential difference of 6 V across it and a current of 2 A through it. What is its resistance?
steps: You want R, so divide both sides by I: R = V ÷ I.
steps.text: Sometimes you need to find the resistance instead. Here is a worked example of that. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see how it is done, one step at a time.
In the same way, to find a current, divide both sides of V = I R by R: I = V ÷ R, current = potential difference ÷ resistance.

steps.prompt: In one line: what do potential difference and resistance each do to the current?
points: a bigger potential difference (push) gives a bigger current
a bigger resistance gives a smaller current
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: a bigger potential difference pushes a bigger current, and a bigger resistance makes the current smaller.

steps.question: Where do you put an ammeter to measure the current in a single loop?

options.text: Across the cell, like a voltmeter

steps.right: Yes. In a single loop the current is the same at every point, so the ammeter can go anywhere in the loop.

wrong.M4: Not quite: anywhere in the loop. The current is the same at every point in a single loop, so the place does not matter.
wrong.M10: Not quite: anywhere in the loop. An ammeter is joined into the loop itself; it is the voltmeter that goes across a component.
wrong.other: Not quite: anywhere in the loop. The current is the same at every point of a single loop.

idk.hint: Think about whether the current in a single loop is different in different places. Where can you put the ammeter to measure the current?

ask.question: Does the current in a single loop change from one point to another?

wrong.other: Not quite.

steps.answerWhy: Anywhere in the loop. The current is the same at every point in a single loop, so it does not matter where the ammeter goes, as long as it is in the loop.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — the resistance of a wire

steps.text: Wire is used in heaters, chargers and the coils inside motors, so engineers need to know how the length of a wire changes its resistance. This is a practical you will do in class; here is how it works.

steps.question: Before the practical, a quick check. What does an ammeter measure?
steps.right: Yes: an ammeter measures the current through a component.

wrong.M8: Not quite: an ammeter measures the current. A voltmeter measures the potential difference.
wrong.other: Not quite: an ammeter measures the current through a component.

idk.hint: An ammeter's name gives a clue: an ammeter shows a reading in amperes. Which quantity is measured in amperes?

steps.answerWhy: An ammeter measures the current, in amperes.

steps.question: How do you work out a resistance from the potential difference V and the current I?

options.text: Divide the potential difference by the current
Divide the current by the potential difference

steps.right: Yes: resistance = potential difference ÷ current, R = V ÷ I.

wrong.other: Not quite: divide the potential difference by the current. R = V ÷ I comes from V = I R.
wrong.upside-down: Not quite: it is the other way up. Divide the potential difference by the current: R = V ÷ I.

idk.hint: Remember V = I R. Which of the three ways gets R on its own?

steps.answerWhy: Divide the potential difference by the current: R = V ÷ I, from V = I R.

steps.text: A long wire is clipped along a metre ruler and joined to a cell. The ammeter is joined in series with the wire: one after another in the same loop, so the same current flows through both.

The voltmeter is joined in parallel with the wire, side by side across the same two points: its two clips go at each end of the length you are testing. The voltmeter measures the potential difference across that length.

steps.question: The voltmeter reads 3 V and the ammeter reads 0.5 A. What is the resistance of this length of wire, in ohms?

wrong.multiplied: Not quite: it's 6 Ω. You multiplied; resistance needs dividing: R = V ÷ I = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6.
wrong.upside-down: Not quite: it's 6 Ω. You divided the current by the potential difference; it is the other way up: R = V ÷ I = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6.
wrong.other: Not quite: it's 6 Ω. R = V ÷ I = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6.

idk.hint: Use R = V ÷ I: the potential difference divided by the current. What is 3 divided by 0.5?

ask.question: How many halves are there in 3?

wrong.other: Not quite.

steps.answerWhy: The resistance is 6 Ω: R = V ÷ I = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6.

steps.text: Next, move one clip to change the length of wire between the clips, and read the ammeter and the voltmeter again. Do this for several different lengths.

steps.question: What do you think happens to the resistance when the length of wire between the clips is longer?
steps.right: Yes. A longer wire has a bigger resistance.

wrong.other: Not quite: it gets bigger. A longer wire has a bigger resistance.

idk.hint: Think of the charge squeezing through the wire. With more wire to get through, does the resistance get bigger, get smaller or stay the same?

steps.answerWhy: The resistance gets bigger: a longer wire has a bigger resistance.

steps.text: Keep the current small and switch off between readings, so the wire does not warm up. As a wire warms, its resistance changes, which would spoil the test. That is why the wire is kept at a constant temperature: its temperature stays the same.
Keeping the current small matters for safety too: a hot wire can burn you. One cell's low potential difference gives no risk of an electric shock.
Repeat each reading and work out the mean: the average of the repeats.
Then plot a graph of resistance against length. The points lie on a straight line through the origin, the point where both length and resistance are zero.

The same circuit can also measure two resistors joined together, either one after the other in the same loop (in series) or side by side (in parallel). For each, measure the potential difference and the current, then divide.

steps.prompt: In one line: how does the length of a wire change its resistance?
points: a longer wire has a bigger resistance
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: a longer wire has a bigger resistance.

steps.question: In the resistance-of-a-wire practical, why does one cell give no risk of an electric shock?
steps.right: Yes. A low potential difference means no risk of an electric shock. The wire can still get hot, so keep the current small.

wrong.other: Not quite: its potential difference is low, and a low potential difference gives no risk of an electric shock.

idk.hint: One cell gives only a small push. Which answer is about the push?

steps.answerWhy: One cell's potential difference is low, and a low potential difference gives no risk of an electric shock.

keyPoints.heading: Ohmic conductors — resistance that stays the same

steps.text: In some components the resistance stays the same as the current changes; in others it changes. To find out which is which, you measure the current at several potential differences and plot a graph.
A graph of current against potential difference is called an I-V characteristic. Current (I) goes up the side and potential difference (V) goes along the bottom.

cv-ohmic-R.tryShort: On the graph, drag the point from 2 V to 4 V. Watch the current and the resistance reading (V ÷ I).
cv-ohmic-R.afterTest: At 4 V the current was twice what it was at 2 V, and the resistance reading did not change.

explain.promptShort: In one line: why do you think the resistance stayed the same?
points: the current doubled when the potential difference doubled
so V ÷ I did not change

steps.text: Predict first: answer the question in the box below. Then a graph of a resistor opens: drag the point along the line to test your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
For a resistor kept at a constant temperature, the points of an I-V characteristic lie on a straight line through the origin.

When the potential difference doubles, the current doubles too. Two quantities that change together like this are directly proportional: here, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference.

A straight line through the origin means the resistance does not change as the current changes. A component whose resistance stays the same like this, at a constant temperature, is called an ohmic conductor.

steps.question: An ohmic conductor has a current of 0.2 A through it at 3 V. What is the current through it at 6 V?
steps.right: Yes: 0.4 A. The potential difference doubled, so the current doubled too.

wrong.M5: Not quite: 0.4 A. The current does not stay the same: for an ohmic conductor it doubles when the potential difference doubles.
wrong.other: Not quite: 0.4 A. The potential difference doubled, from 3 V to 6 V, so the current doubled, from 0.2 A to 0.4 A.

idk.hint: From 3 V to 6 V, the potential difference has doubled. For an ohmic conductor, the current is directly proportional to it. What is the current at 6 V?

wrong.other: Not quite.

steps.answerWhy: The current is 0.4 A: the potential difference doubled, so the current doubled too, from 0.2 A to 0.4 A.

steps.text: For an ohmic conductor you can use V = I R with one fixed value of R, whatever the current.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does a straight-line I-V graph through the origin tell you?
points: the current is directly proportional to the potential difference
the resistance stays the same
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the current is directly proportional to the potential difference, so the resistance stays the same.

steps.question: What is the unit of resistance?
steps.right: Yes: resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

wrong.other: Not quite: resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). Volts are for potential difference and amperes for current.

idk.hint: The unit of resistance has the symbol Ω. What is the unit called?

steps.answerWhy: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

keyPoints.heading: Filament lamps and diodes — resistance that changes

steps.text: Not every component gives a straight line. Some give curves, and the shape of the curve tells you what is happening inside the component.
An old-style bulb is a filament lamp.
Inside a filament lamp is a thin coil of metal wire, called the filament, that glows white-hot.
As the current through a filament lamp rises, the filament gets hotter, and its resistance increases as its temperature increases.

steps.question: A filament lamp is glowing brightly. You turn the potential difference down, so the filament cools. What happens to its resistance?
steps.right: Yes. A cooler filament has a smaller resistance.

wrong.other: Not quite: it decreases. A hotter filament has a bigger resistance, so a cooler one has a smaller resistance.
wrong.M12: Not quite: it decreases. A filament lamp is not an ohmic conductor: as it cools, its resistance goes down.

idk.hint: Hotter means a bigger resistance. What do you think cooler means?

steps.answerWhy: The filament's resistance decreases: a hotter filament has a bigger resistance, so a cooler one has a smaller resistance.

steps.text: Back to turning the potential difference up: as the filament heats and its resistance goes up, each extra volt pushes less extra current through the lamp than the volt before. The graph bends over and gets flatter.
How steep a line on a graph is is called its gradient. The filament lamp's line gets flatter, so its gradient decreases.
Try it: below is the filament lamp's graph. Drag the point from 2 V up to 6 V and watch the resistance reading (V ÷ I). Tap Next when you are done.
On a curved graph, the resistance is different at different points. To find the resistance at one point, read off V and I there, then divide V by I.
Next, a diode: a component used in chargers and other electronics. In a circuit drawing, a diode is a triangle pointing at a short bar.
Turning a component round makes the potential difference push the other way. On an I-V graph, readings taken like this go on the left of zero, as a negative potential difference.

cv-diode.question: A diode is joined into a loop with a cell and an ammeter, and a current flows. Then the diode is turned round. What happens to the current?

options.text: It flows the other way, just as big
options.short: It flows the other way, just as big

cv-diode.tryShort: On the diode graph, the point is at a negative potential difference: that is the diode turned round. Read the current. Then drag the point to the right of zero.
cv-diode.afterTest: Turned round, the current was almost 0 A. The other way round, the current rose.

explain.promptShort: In one line: what did you see when the diode was turned round?
points: almost no current flowed
the other way round, the current rose

steps.text: Predict first: answer the question in the box below. Then drag the point on the diode's graph to test your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
A diode lets current flow in one direction only. Turned round, almost no current flows, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

On the diode's graph, the left side (turned round, the reverse direction) lies flat along the axis. On the right side (the forward direction), the current stays near zero at first, then rises steeply. The filament lamp's graph has the same shape on both sides.

steps.prompt: In one line: how are a filament lamp and a diode different from a resistor?
points: their I-V graphs are not straight lines
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: their I-V graphs are not straight lines.

steps.question: Which component lets current flow in one direction only?
steps.right: Yes: a diode. Its resistance is very high in the reverse direction.

wrong.other: Not quite: a diode. Its resistance is very high in the reverse direction, so current flows one way only.

idk.hint: Think of the graph that lay flat along the axis on one side. Which component was that?

steps.answerWhy: A diode lets current flow in one direction only: its resistance is very high in the reverse direction.

steps.question: Before the practical, a quick check. Which meter goes in parallel across the component you are testing?
steps.right: Yes: the voltmeter goes in parallel, to measure the potential difference across the component.

wrong.M10: Not quite: the voltmeter. The ammeter goes in series, in the loop, so the current flows through it.
wrong.other: Not quite: only the voltmeter. The ammeter goes in series, in the loop.

idk.hint: The meter that goes in parallel measures the potential difference across the component. Which meter is that?

steps.answerWhy: The voltmeter goes in parallel across the component; the ammeter goes in series.

steps.question: What does a straight-line I-V graph through the origin show?
steps.right: Yes: the resistance stays the same. It is an ohmic conductor.

wrong.other: Not quite: the resistance stays the same. A straight line through the origin means an ohmic conductor.

idk.hint: Think of the resistor at constant temperature. Did its resistance change along its straight-line graph?

steps.answerWhy: The resistance stays the same: a straight line through the origin means an ohmic conductor.

steps.text: Here is how you measure an I-V characteristic in class, step by step. The circuit has a cell or a battery (two or more cells joined together) and the component you are testing. The ammeter is in series with the component, and the voltmeter is in parallel across it.
The loop also has a variable resistor: a resistor whose resistance you can change with a slider. Moving the slider changes the current, so you get a range of readings.
Instead of a variable resistor, you can change the number of cells, or use a supply whose potential difference you can set.

steps.question: To make the current small at the start, do you set the variable resistor to its highest or its lowest resistance?
steps.right: Yes: its highest resistance, so the current starts small.

wrong.other: Not quite: its highest resistance, so the current starts small.

idk.hint: A bigger resistance gives a smaller current. Which setting gives the smallest current?

steps.answerWhy: Set it to its highest resistance, so the current starts small.

steps.text: Record the current and the potential difference, then move the slider and record both again.
Take readings at even steps across the range, and repeat them, as in the wire practical. Take care with a filament lamp: it gets very hot, so do not touch it.
For the left-hand half of the graph, turn the component round and take the readings again. Those readings count as negative.
A component whose I-V graph is a straight line is called linear.

steps.question: Which of these components is linear?
steps.right: Yes: a resistor at constant temperature gives a straight line.

wrong.other: Not quite: the resistor at constant temperature. Its graph is a straight line; the filament lamp and the diode give curves.

idk.hint: Linear means a straight-line graph. Which of the three gave a straight line?

steps.answerWhy: A resistor at constant temperature: its I-V graph is a straight line.

steps.text: A component whose graph is not a straight line is called non-linear, so the filament lamp and the diode are non-linear.
The shape of a graph shows how a component's resistance behaves, and so what the component is useful for. A diode, for example, can stop current flowing the wrong way.

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you take the readings for an I-V graph?
points: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel
change the current with a variable resistor
turn the component round for the negative readings
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel; change the current with a variable resistor; turn the component round for the negative readings.

steps.question: Why do you keep the current small in the resistance-of-a-wire practical?

options.text: So the wire does not warm up

steps.right: Yes. A small current keeps the wire at a constant temperature.

wrong.other: Not quite: so the wire does not warm up. A small current keeps it at a constant temperature.

idk.hint: Which of the answers is about the wire's temperature?

steps.answerWhy: You keep the current small so the wire does not warm up: a small current keeps it at a constant temperature.

keyPoints.heading: Energy transferred — what the charge carries

steps.text: Energy is measured in a unit called the joule, written J.

cv-flat-cell.tryShort: Tap Run for 10 s a few times. Compare the charge that left the cell with the charge that came back.
cv-flat-cell.afterTest: The charge that came back to the cell was the same as the charge that left it, while the energy passed to the lamp kept going up.

points: the charge is not used up

steps.text: Predict first: answer the question in the box below. Then run the circuit for 10 seconds at a time to test your answer. Tap Next when you are done.
A cell does more than push charge round a circuit: it gives energy to the charge. The charge hands that energy over in the components, lighting a lamp, warming a heater or turning a motor.
When charge flows through a component, energy is passed from the charge to the component. Physicists call this work done.
The amount of energy passed on is called the energy transferred, measured in joules.

The push of a potential difference is really about energy: the potential difference across a component tells you how much energy each coulomb transfers there. A potential difference of 1 volt means 1 joule is transferred for each coulomb that passes.

steps.question: A lamp has a potential difference of 12 V across it. How many joules does each coulomb of charge transfer in the lamp?
steps.right: Yes: 12 J for each coulomb. 12 V means 12 joules for every coulomb.

wrong.other: Not quite: 12 J. A potential difference of 12 V means 12 joules for every coulomb that passes.

idk.hint: 1 volt means 1 joule for each coulomb. How many joules is that for each coulomb at 12 volts?

steps.answerWhy: Each coulomb transfers 12 J: a potential difference of 12 V means 12 joules for every coulomb.

steps.text: To find the total energy transferred, use E = Q V: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference. E is the energy transferred in joules (J), Q is the charge flow in coulombs (C) and V is the potential difference in volts (V).
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see how it is done, one step at a time.
steps.question: 3 C of charge flows through a lamp with a potential difference of 6 V across it. How much energy is transferred?
steps: Write the equation: E = Q V.

steps.text: If you are given a current and a time instead of a charge, find the charge first with Q = I t. Then use E = Q V.
Here is a worked example with both steps. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see how it is done.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does a potential difference of 1 volt mean?

steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: 1 volt means 1 joule of energy is transferred for each coulomb of charge that passes.

steps.question: When charge flows through a lamp, what happens to the charge and to its energy?

options.text: The charge carries on round; its energy goes to the lamp
The charge is used up in the lamp
Nothing happens to either of them

steps.right: Yes. The charge carries on round the circuit, and its energy is transferred to the lamp.

wrong.M6: Not quite: the charge is not used up. It carries on round the circuit; its energy is what goes to the lamp.
wrong.other: Not quite: the charge carries on round, and its energy is transferred to the lamp.

idk.hint: Think of the circuit you ran for 10 seconds: did the charge come back to the cell? What kept going up?

steps.answerWhy: The charge carries on round the circuit, and its energy is transferred to the lamp.

steps.text: To finish, a short quiz on the whole lesson: 8 questions.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 8: What is electric current?

options.text: How much charge passes a point each second
How hard it is for charge to flow

steps.right: Yes. Current is how much charge passes a point each second.

wrong.M8: Not quite: the push that drives charge is the potential difference. Current is how much charge passes a point each second.
wrong.resistance: Not quite: how hard it is for charge to flow is the resistance. Current is how much charge passes a point each second.
wrong.other: Not quite. Current is how much charge passes a point each second.

steps.answerWhy: Current is how much charge passes a point each second.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 8: Which equation links charge flow, current and time?
steps.right: Yes. Q = I t: charge flow = current × time.

wrong.other: Not quite. Q = I t: charge flow = current × time.

steps.answerWhy: Q = I t: charge flow = current × time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 8: What does the I-V characteristic of an ohmic conductor look like?

options.text: A straight line through the origin
Flat on one side, steep on the other

steps.right: Yes. A straight line through the origin: its current is directly proportional to the potential difference.

wrong.other: Not quite. A straight line through the origin: its current is directly proportional to the potential difference.

steps.answerWhy: A straight line through the origin: its current is directly proportional to the potential difference.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 8: Why does a filament lamp's I-V graph curve?

options.text: Its resistance increases as it gets hotter
It lets current flow one way only
Its resistance falls as it gets hotter

steps.right: Yes. A filament lamp's resistance increases as it gets hotter, so the line gets flatter.

wrong.other: Not quite. A filament lamp's resistance increases as it gets hotter, so the line gets flatter.

steps.answerWhy: A filament lamp's resistance increases as it gets hotter, so the line gets flatter.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 8: In the I-V practical, how is the voltmeter connected?
steps.right: Yes. In parallel across the component, to measure the potential difference across it.

wrong.M10: Not quite. In parallel across the component, to measure the potential difference across it.
wrong.M9: Not quite. In parallel across the component, to measure the potential difference across it.
wrong.other: Not quite. In parallel across the component, to measure the potential difference across it.

steps.answerWhy: In parallel across the component, to measure the potential difference across it.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 8: At constant temperature, what happens to a wire's resistance as its length increases?
steps.right: Yes. A wire's resistance increases: a longer wire has a bigger resistance.

wrong.other: Not quite. A wire's resistance increases: a longer wire has a bigger resistance.

steps.answerWhy: A wire's resistance increases: a longer wire has a bigger resistance.
